decision.reason: Under Step 2, nonexclusive conceptual retests of specific attributed empirical findings qualify as replications, and a paper need not retest every manipulation in an original article. Although Section II.F notes the experience tests are not directly tied to one specific study and revisit a broader stylized fact, it immediately names Hussam, Porter, and Smith (2008) under 'Replication Tests of the Experience Effect' as one of two explicit empirical comparators for testing whether trading experience reduces RD, RDMAX, and RAD between the first and second market repetitions. Inspecting the complete published Hussam et al. (2008, AER 98(3):924-937; hussam.txt) confirms that alongside their novel liquidity/dividend-variance 'rekindling' manipulation (Result 1 second sentence & Result 5, pp. 932, 936, not manipulated here), Hussam et al. explicitly test stationary baseline/replication SSW sessions across experience levels and report Result 1 (first sentence, p. 932: 'Experience reduces the amplitude of a bubble significantly') and Result 2 (p. 934: 'Experience significantly reduces the duration of a bubble'). Even though Hussam et al. p. 930 note their baseline sessions replicate SSW (1988), Huber et al. explicitly cite and compare their two-repetition test against Hussam, Porter, and Smith's (2008) published baseline experience-attenuation finding.

decision.reason: Evaluating the outcome strictly for the retested stationary experience-attenuation finding of Hussam, Porter, and Smith (2008) (Result 1 first part and Result 2, AER 98(3):932-934, showing that experience significantly reduces bubble amplitude and duration across stationary repetitions, whereas Hussam et al.'s rekindling treatment under environment shocks is outside the scope of Huber et al.'s constant-parameter design), Huber et al. (2024) test whether RD, RDMAX, and RAD decrease significantly from the first to the second market repetition across n = 166 paired markets. All three preregistered paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank robustness tests are highly significant in the same direction (RD: t(165) = 8.236, p < 0.001; RDMAX: t(165) = 8.566, p < 0.001; RAD: t(165) = 7.134, p < 0.001), which the authors explicitly summarize as 'implying a replication rate of 100% for the experience hypothesis according to the statistical significance indicator' and in Section III (p. 38) as 'our replications corroborated the stylized fact that experience curbs the extent of bubbles'. Although one-sample tests show overpricing is not completely eliminated in repetition 2 (t(165) = 8.316, p < 0.001), the retested attenuation claim is unambiguously successful.

decision.reason: In Section II.F, Huber et al. (2024)—which includes original co-authors Jürgen Huber and Michael Kirchler—explicitly cite Sutter, Huber, and Kirchler (2012, Management Science 58(2):384-393, doi:10.1287/mnsc.1110.1365) alongside Hussam et al. (2008) as the specific empirical comparator for testing whether trading experience reduces RD, RDMAX, and RAD between market repetitions, while also stating the experience test is not directly tied to one specific study. However, verifying the exact original-specific finding chain in the published 2012 article is blocked by genuine primary-source incompleteness: only the publisher abstract (sutter_published_browser.txt, which mentions only asymmetric information effects on bubbles and not repetition/experience) and the 2008 working paper (sutter_wp.txt, which runs three 10-period rounds and finds significant round-3 overvaluation reduction in Table 2, p. 18, plus a Round 3 Control vs. Round 1 Insider comparison on p. 10) are available, and version equivalence between the 2008 working paper and the 2012 published article is not established. Because the abstract's silence does not disprove the 2012 full text containing the repetition finding attributed by Huber et al., yet the 2008 WP cannot unconditionally stand in for the 2012 article's exact RD/RDMAX/RAD claims, original target status is undeterminable.

(2024) report a 100% statistically significant reduction in RD (t(165) = 8.236, p < 0.001), RDMAX (t(165) = 8.566, p < 0.001), and RAD (t(165) = 7.134, p < 0.001) between the first and second market repetitions (and Section III p. 38 states that their replications corroborated the experience effect), determining the replication outcome for Row 431 depends on verifying the exact original claim and finding chain in the published Sutter, Huber, and Kirchler (2012, Management Science 58(2):384-393) article. Because the published 2012 full text is unavailable—only the publisher abstract (sutter_published_browser.txt, which describes only information-asymmetry effects) and the 2008 working paper (sutter_wp.txt, where Table 2 p. 18 shows Round 2 dummy -2.44 insignificant and Round 3 dummy -4.38*** significant on price-fundamental spreads, without established version equivalence to the 2012 published article's RD/RDMAX/RAD first-vs-second repetition tests)—the exact original finding level and whether it is a valid standalone target row or how its specific repetition results compare cannot be verified from primary evidence. Thus, outcome is undeterminable (null).
